K-418.h1: Picture Tracing Worksheets: Trace the Garden Path to the Door
K-418.title: Picture Tracing Worksheets: The Garden Path to the Door | PDF
K-418.metaDescription: Trace a whole garden along dashed lines: a cottage, a big tree, tulips, a rabbit and a path that leads to the door. A picture tracing page for kindergarten. PDF.
K-418.p1: This page is one complete picture, not a row of separate drawings. A cottage with a chimney and a round window stands on a gently rolling hill, a big tree spreads its crown beside it, a butterfly flies between the roof and the leaves, and a garden path runs from the bottom edge of the page up to the front door. Two tulips stand at the mouth of the path like a gateway, a rabbit sits on the grass, and a cloud and a sun fill the sky. Every line is dashed, and when the last dash is traced the garden is finished.
K-418.p2: Tracing a whole scene asks for more than steady strokes. The child has to choose where to start, follow long lines like the hill and the path from one side to the other, close round shapes like the sun and the windows, and keep going picture by picture until nothing is left grey. The dashes lie exactly on the drawing's own lines, so there is nothing to erase and nothing to guess. Small details such as the sun's rays and the grass tufts are already drawn, so the effort goes into the lines that matter. Talk about the garden while tracing: who lives in the house, where does the path go?
K-418.p3: The worksheet prints as a single PDF page with room for the child's name and the date. It suits kindergarten and the end of preschool, and it works well as a calm start to the day or a quiet table activity. When this page is easy, try the dotted town street for finer lines, or the forest page where five dashed animals hide among solid trees. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-419.h1: Tracing Worksheets for Preschool: My First Big Whale
K-419.title: Tracing Worksheets for Preschool: My First Big Whale | PDF
K-419.metaDescription: One giant whale to trace with long, slow lines, starting at a dot. A first picture tracing page for preschool hands, seen through a ship's round window. PDF.
K-419.p1: A first tracing page should give a small hand one big, friendly job, and that is all this page does. A whale almost as wide as the page swims across the inside of a ship's round porthole. Its outline is drawn in thick, well-spaced dashes, and a solid dot with a small arrow on its back shows where to begin. The waves at the bottom, the bubbles and the rim of the porthole are already drawn in solid black, so the only grey line on the page is the whale itself.
K-419.p2: Three- and four-year-olds are still learning to hold a crayon and to keep it moving along a line. Long, gently curving strokes are the easiest place to practice that, much easier than small corners or tiny details. The whale's eye, mouth and belly stripes are printed solid so the child is never asked to trace a line too short or too close to the next one. Let the child run a finger along the whale first, then trace slowly with a thick crayon, and praise a line that keeps going rather than a line that is perfect.
K-419.p3: This printable PDF is meant for preschool and for any child who is just beginning to trace. It pairs well with the look-then-trace page, where a penguin and a kangaroo are traced next to a solid model, and with the round-and-round page of big circles. After that the kindergarten pages add more pictures and thinner lines. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-420.h1: Trace the Picture: Look at the Animal, Then Trace It
K-420.title: Trace the Picture: Look at the Animal, Then Trace It | PDF
K-420.metaDescription: A penguin and a kangaroo shown as finished photos, each with a big dashed copy to trace beside it. Look first, then trace: a preschool tracing page. PDF.
K-420.p1: Each row of this page has two halves. On the left a small finished picture sits in a photo frame with an eye badge on top: a penguin in the first row, a kangaroo in the second. On the right, after an arrow, the same animal is drawn large in thick dashes, waiting to be traced. The model is solid and framed, so it is clear which picture is for looking and which one is for the crayon, and the dashed copy is the same drawing facing the same way.
K-420.p2: Looking at a model and then making your own copy is the next step after tracing alone, and young children need to practice both parts. The eye badge invites a moment of looking: where are the penguin's wings, how long are the kangaroo's ears? Then the child traces the big copy, starting at the dot on top of the head. Because the copy matches the model line for line, the child can check the finished tracing against the photo and see that it is the same animal. Small parts such as eyelashes stay solid so the lines left to trace are long enough for small hands.
K-420.p3: The page prints as a PDF and suits preschool and the start of kindergarten. Use it after the first big whale page and before pages with several pictures. Children who enjoy it can go on to the other-half page, where they finish the missing half of a butterfly, an owl, a bell and a koala. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-421.h1: Tracing Worksheets for Toddlers: Round and Round Pictures
K-421.title: Tracing Worksheets for Toddlers: Round and Round Pictures | PDF
K-421.metaDescription: A beach ball, an orange and an apple resting on ramps, each with a start dot. Trace round and round, like the letter o: big curves for toddlers. Printable PDF.
K-421.p1: Three round things roll down this page like marbles on a run: a beach ball on the top ramp, an orange on the middle ramp and an apple on the bottom one. Each picture is big, and only its round outline is dashed. The stripes on the ball, the leaves and the stalks are already drawn. On every outline a dot sits near the top right with a small arrow pointing up and to the left, showing the child where to start and which way to go round.
K-421.p2: Going round anticlockwise from the top right is exactly how the letters o, c, a and d begin in every school script, so a child who traces these pictures is already practising the first movement of writing. The pictures are large because young children control big movements before small ones, and the dashes are thick and spaced for a chunky crayon. Encourage the child to start at the dot every time and to come all the way back to it, closing the circle. If a line wobbles, that is fine: the shape is the lesson, not the neatness.
K-421.p3: This printable PDF suits toddlers and preschoolers who have tried a first tracing page. After it, the curls and spirals page adds snails and lollipops that turn and turn again, and the straight-line page practices lines that go down, across and slanted. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-422.h1: Straight-Line Picture Tracing: Down, Across and Slanted
K-422.title: Straight-Line Picture Tracing: Down, Across and Slanted | PDF
K-422.metaDescription: Six pictures made of straight lines in three columns: a ladder and a cabinet, a table and a dresser, an envelope and a sailboat. Kindergarten tracing. PDF.
K-422.p1: The page is divided into three columns, and a round badge at the top of each one shows an arrow. The first column points down and holds a ladder and a cabinet, pictures made mostly of tall lines. The middle column points across and holds a table and a chest of drawers, full of flat lines. The last column points on a slant and holds an envelope and a sailboat, where the flap and the sail are made of slanted lines. Every picture is drawn in dashes and built almost only from straight lines.
K-422.p2: Children learn straight lines in a set order: first down, then across, then slanted, and a slanted line is the hardest of the three. This page follows that order from left to right, so the child practices each direction in a real picture rather than in a row of abstract strokes. The vertical lines of the ladder prepare l and t, the flat lines of the table prepare E and the crossbar of t, and the slants of the sail prepare v, w and k. Ask the child to say the direction aloud while tracing: down, across, slanted.
K-422.p3: This printable PDF suits kindergarten and children who already trace round shapes with ease. It sits naturally between the round-and-round page and the zigzag page, where slanted lines meet in sharp points. Every picture here was measured to be at least seventy percent straight lines. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-423.h1: Trace the Picture: Zigzag Mountains and a Stormy Camp
K-423.title: Trace the Picture: Zigzag Mountains and a Stormy Camp | PDF
K-423.metaDescription: An evening storm over a mountain camp: zigzag peaks, three fir trees with zigzag sides, a tent and lightning. Trace each zigzag and stop at every point. PDF.
K-423.p1: Evening has come to a camp in the mountains. A row of sharp peaks crosses the page from edge to edge, a storm cloud with lightning and raindrops hangs over the middle valley, and a star and a moon shine in the corners of the sky. Below the mountains three fir trees stand on the ground, each with three zigzag tiers, and a tent waits for the campers between them. Every line of the scene is dashed: the peaks, the trees, the tent, the cloud and the lightning bolts.
K-423.p2: A zigzag is two slanted lines that meet in a point, and the skill is to stop at the point and change direction instead of rounding it off. That is exactly the movement needed later for letters such as v, w, k and z. On this page the zigzags are part of real things, the mountains and the fir trees, so the child practices them with a reason to keep going. Remind the child to pause at the top of every peak and at the tip of every branch, then set off in the new direction. The points are wide apart, so there is room to stop.
K-423.p3: This printable PDF suits kindergarten, after the straight-line page and before the curls and spirals page. It also makes a good autumn or camping-week activity, and the finished picture is ready to color. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-424.h1: Tracing Pictures for Kids: Curls and Spirals
K-424.title: Tracing Pictures for Kids: Curls and Spirals Gallery | PDF
K-424.metaDescription: A gallery of five curly pictures to trace: a snail shell, a swirl lollipop, a bow, a pretzel and a pinwheel. Curls and loops for kindergarten. Printable PDF.
K-424.p1: This page is laid out like a small gallery with five framed pictures, and every picture is made of curls. The biggest frame holds a smiling snail whose shell winds round and round to the middle. Next to it a tall lollipop swirls from its edge to its center. Below them a bow loops out on both sides, a pretzel twists into its three holes, and a pinwheel turns its blades around a little circle. All five pictures are drawn in dashes, ready to be traced one frame at a time.
K-424.p2: A curl turns and turns again without stopping, and following it asks the hand to keep a steady, rounded movement over a long distance. That movement is the base of loops in joined handwriting and of letters such as e and l. Spirals are the hardest part, so the turns of the snail shell and the lollipop are spaced wide enough for a child's pencil. Tiny details, such as the salt on the pretzel, are printed solid, so the child is never asked to trace a mark smaller than a fingertip. Work frame by frame and let the child choose the order.
K-424.p3: This printable PDF suits kindergarten and confident preschoolers who have already traced round pictures. It follows the zigzag page in the set and leads on to the trace-and-color picnic. Each finished frame also makes a lovely little picture to color in. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-425.h1: Trace and Color the Picture: A Picnic Under the Tree
K-425.title: Trace and Color the Picture: A Picnic Under the Tree | PDF
K-425.metaDescription: Trace a picnic under a tree, then color the watermelon, the cup, the pear and the lemon inside the lines. Big shapes to trace and color. Kindergarten PDF.
K-425.p1: A picnic blanket lies on the grass under a big leafy tree. On the blanket there is a whole watermelon, a cup of tea, a pear and a lemon, and a little bird sits in the air between the tree and the sun. A cloud drifts across the sky. Everything on the page is drawn in dashed lines, and every shape is closed, so once it has been traced it becomes a space ready to color in. There are no numbers and no color codes: the child chooses the colors.
K-425.p2: This page practices two different kinds of control in one sitting. First the child traces, keeping the crayon on the line. Then the child colors, keeping the crayon inside the line. The big, calm shapes of the fruit and the blanket make the second step manageable, and the closed outlines give every color a clear edge to stop at. Finishing a page you have both drawn and colored is satisfying, and it turns tracing practice into a picture a child is proud to take home or hang on the wall.
K-425.p3: This printable PDF suits kindergarten and the end of preschool. If you want coloring with a rule, the shape rocket page asks for every circle to be colored; on this picnic page the child chooses every color. For more practice with closed shapes, try the Christmas page with its many baubles. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-426.h1: Picture Tracing for Kindergarten: Where Do I Start?
K-426.title: Picture Tracing for Kindergarten: Where Do I Start? | PDF
K-426.metaDescription: Four simple pictures on a staircase: a flag, a heart, a stocking and a bell. Every line has a start dot and an arrow. Learn where to start. Kindergarten PDF.
K-426.p1: A staircase runs down the page from the top left corner to the bottom right, and on every step there is one simple picture: a flag at the top, then a heart, a stocking and a bell at the bottom. Each picture is made of only two or three lines. Every line begins with a solid dot and has a small arrow beside it showing which way to go, and a sample dot and arrow in the top corner explains the sign. Where two lines start at the same point, they share one dot with two arrows.
K-426.p2: Knowing where to start a line and which way to go is the habit that later makes letters easy to form. On this page every line starts at its top or left end, and round lines start near the top right and go round anticlockwise, the same rules children meet in handwriting. The pictures were drawn stroke by stroke for this purpose, so there are no confusing extra lines. Ask the child to put a finger on each dot first, follow the arrow with the finger, and only then trace. Work down the stairs one step at a time.
K-426.p3: This printable PDF suits kindergarten and children who are getting ready to write letters. It is deliberately light, because the lesson is the order of the lines rather than their length. Afterwards, any page in the set can be traced with the same habit: find the start, follow the direction. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-427.h1: Trace and Count: How Many Ducks Are on the Pond?
K-427.title: Trace and Count: How Many Ducks Are on the Pond? | PDF
K-427.metaDescription: Trace the ducks swimming on a village pond, count them and write how many in the box. A frog and a turtle sit on the bank. Tracing and counting for K. PDF.
K-427.p1: A big oval pond fills the lower part of the page, and five ducks swim on it, some facing left and some facing right. The ducks are drawn in dashes. On the bank above the water there is a tree, a frog and a turtle, all drawn in solid lines, with a cloud in the sky and reeds at the water's edge. In the top corner an empty box with a writing line waits for the answer. Only the ducks are dashed, so the page itself shows which animals to trace and count.
K-427.p2: Tracing each duck before counting it slows the child down and turns every duck into one clear thing to count. Because the ducks are scattered around the pond rather than standing in a line, the child has to keep track of which ones have already been counted, which is the real counting skill for kindergarten: count up to ten objects in a scattered arrangement and answer how many. The frog and the turtle are there on purpose. They are a different kind of animal and are not dashed, so the child learns to count only what the question asks about.
K-427.p3: This printable PDF suits kindergarten math and fine-motor time at once, and it works well with a small group: trace, count together, then write the number. The answer is five, and the number is written by the child, so there is no key to check. For more figure-and-ground looking, try the forest page with five hidden animals. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-428.h1: Picture Tracing Sheets: Finish the Picture
K-428.title: Picture Tracing Sheets: Finish the Picture on the Shelf | PDF
K-428.metaDescription: Six pictures on two shelves, each missing a part: car wheels, a teapot spout, an umbrella handle, a cup handle, a top's point, bunny ears. Trace to finish. PDF.
K-428.p1: Two shelves stretch across the page under a row of bunting, and six things wait on them to be mended. On the top shelf there is a toy car, a teapot and an umbrella; on the bottom shelf a cup on its saucer, a spinning top and a bunny. Each picture is drawn in solid lines except for one part, which is dashed: the car's wheels, the teapot's spout, the umbrella's handle, the cup's handle, the point of the top and the bunny's long ears. Tracing that part makes the picture whole.
K-428.p2: To finish a picture the child first has to see what is missing, and that looking is as important as the tracing. Ask before tracing: what does the teapot need? Where are the bunny's ears? The missing parts are real, nameable parts rather than random gaps, so the child can talk about them, and each one is long enough to trace properly. Seeing a whole thing in a part of it, and adding the part that completes it, is a skill children use when they read letters and recognize shapes.
K-428.p3: This printable PDF suits kindergarten and is a good change from pages where everything is dashed, because most of each picture is already drawn and the child adds only the finishing touch. For a page where a whole half is missing, try the other-half page with a butterfly in an open book. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-429.h1: Christmas Picture Tracing: Close Every Bauble on the Tree
K-429.title: Christmas Picture Tracing: Close Every Bauble on the Tree | PDF
K-429.metaDescription: A cozy living room on Christmas Eve: a tree with round baubles and stars, gifts, an armchair and a night window with a moon. Trace and close every shape. PDF.
K-429.p1: It is Christmas Eve in a cozy living room. A tall Christmas tree in a pot stands in the middle with a star on top, and round baubles and little stars hang on its branches. Two wrapped gifts sit beside it, an armchair waits in the corner, and through the window a moon and stars shine in the night sky. The scene is indoors, with no snow, so it fits every family's Christmas, in winter or in summer. Every line of the room and the tree is dashed.
K-429.p2: The real practice on this page is in the small shapes. Each bauble and each star is a closed shape that has to end exactly where it began, and there are about a dozen of them, small but well spaced. Closing small round shapes is the movement children need for letters such as a, d, g and o, and the festive setting makes the repetition feel like decorating the tree rather than doing exercises. After tracing, the baubles are perfect for coloring in bright colors.
K-429.p3: This printable PDF suits kindergarten and makes a calm December activity for class or home. Pair it with the trace-and-color picnic for more coloring, or with the summer postcard if your Christmas falls in summer. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-430.h1: Shape Picture Tracing: A Rocket of Circles, Squares and Triangles
K-430.title: Shape Picture Tracing: A Rocket of Circles and Squares | PDF
K-430.metaDescription: A rocket and a sky built only from true shapes: circles, squares, triangles and rectangles in different sizes and turns. Trace, then color every circle. K PDF.
K-430.p1: A rocket stands on its launch pad in the middle of the page, and every part of it is a true shape. Its body is a tall rectangle, its nose is a triangle, its two windows are circles, its hatch is a square, its fins are triangles and its flame is a triangle pointing down. Around the rocket the sky holds more shapes: a big round moon, a small planet, a square turned on its point and another square standing upright. A small key in the corner shows a filled circle.
K-430.p2: Children first learn shapes in one standard position, and then have to learn that a shape keeps its name when it is bigger, smaller or turned. This page shows the same shapes in different sizes and positions, so the circles are big and small and one square stands on its corner. Tracing each shape helps the child feel its corners and sides, and the second task, coloring every circle, asks the child to find all the circles wherever they are. A square turned on its corner is still a square, and that is worth saying aloud.
K-430.p3: This printable PDF suits kindergarten geometry and fine-motor practice together. The rocket contains thirteen shapes, all drawn exactly, with no rounded corners and no ovals. For coloring in any colors after tracing, try the picnic page; for straight lines in real pictures, the down, across and slanted page. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-431.h1: Summer Picture Tracing: Trace the Waves Across the Sea
K-431.title: Summer Picture Tracing: Trace the Waves Across the Sea | PDF
K-431.metaDescription: A seaside postcard with a stamp: trace the horizon and two long waves from left to right, then the sailboat, parasol, bucket, sandcastle and crab. K PDF.
K-431.p1: The page is a postcard from the seaside, with a double border and a stamp showing an anchor in the top corner. A sun shines over the sea, and a straight horizon runs across the page from one side to the other. Below it two long waves roll across the whole width, and a sailboat floats on the first wave. On the beach there is a parasol, a bucket with a spade, a sandcastle with flags and a crab. Everything except the postcard frame and the stamp is dashed.
K-431.p2: The long lines are the heart of this page. Tracing a line all the way from the left edge to the right edge, without stopping, is the same movement as writing along a line of text, and it asks the hand to cross the middle of the body, which young children find harder than it looks. The horizon is straight and the waves go up and down evenly, so the child practices both kinds of long line. After the sea comes the fun part: the beach pictures, each one closed and ready to color.
K-431.p3: This printable PDF suits kindergarten and is a cheerful page for the end of the school year or a summer holiday at home. It sits after the Christmas page in the set and before the big, middle and small page. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

K-432.h1: Tracing Pictures for Kids: Big, Middle and Small
K-432.title: Tracing Pictures for Kids: Big, Middle and Small Vehicles | PDF
K-432.metaDescription: Three rows of vehicles, each drawn big, middle and small: airplanes in the sky, cars on the road, ships on the sea. Trace from big to small. Kindergarten PDF.
K-432.p1: The page has three rows, and each row shows the same vehicle three times, getting smaller from left to right. At the top three airplanes fly under a little cloud, in the middle three cars drive along a road, and at the bottom three ships sail on the waves. The biggest copy in each row is drawn in thick dashes, the middle copy in medium dashes and the smallest in fine dashes, so the line gets thinner as the picture shrinks.
K-432.p2: Being able to make the same shape bigger or smaller is an important part of pencil control, and it is the skill children need later to write letters that fit their lines. Tracing the big airplane uses the whole arm; tracing the small one needs small, careful finger movements. Doing all three in a row lets the child feel the difference. Ask the child to start with the big one each time, and to compare the three finished pictures: they are the same airplane, only bigger and smaller.
K-432.p3: This printable PDF suits kindergarten and is a favorite with children who love vehicles. When the small copies feel easy, the dotted town street page asks for even finer, more careful lines. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

G1-429.h1: Dotted Picture Tracing for 1st Grade: A Town Street
G1-429.title: Dotted Picture Tracing for 1st Grade: Morning on a Town Street | PDF
G1-429.metaDescription: A whole town street drawn in small, even dots: a museum, a hotel, a signpost, a dog, a bus and a car. Trace every dot, details too. For 1st grade. PDF.
G1-429.p1: Morning has come to a little town street. A museum with columns and a big hotel with many windows stand on the pavement, a signpost points two ways, a dog trots along, and on the road below a bus and a car drive by under a small cloud. The whole picture is drawn in small round dots, evenly spaced across the entire page, from the hotel's windows to the wheels of the bus. There are no dashes here: every line is a row of dots.
G1-429.p2: Dots ask for more precision than dashes. The child has to keep the pencil exactly on a narrow path of small points and follow it into the details: the columns of the museum, the windows of the hotel, the spokes of the signpost and the dog's ears. This is the most detailed page in the set, made for first graders whose pencil grip is now steady. Because the dots have one spacing across the whole page, the child can settle into a rhythm. Encourage slow, careful tracing and short breaks; finishing the whole street is a real achievement.
G1-429.p3: This printable PDF suits first grade and children who have already traced the kindergarten pages with ease. Afterwards the finished street is a wonderful picture to color. For the same precision with a challenge of looking, try the forest page with five hidden animals. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

G1-430.h1: Trace the Picture, Say Its Name and Trace the Word
G1-430.title: Trace the Picture, Say Its Name and Trace the Word | PDF
G1-430.metaDescription: Four picture cards: a sun, a fish, a cat and an apple. Trace each picture, say its name, then trace the word on the writing lines below it. 1st grade PDF.
G1-430.p1: Four picture cards fill the page in two rows. The first card shows a sun, the second a fish, the third a cat and the fourth an apple. Each picture is drawn in fine dashes, and under it, on a set of writing lines, the picture's name is printed in dashed school letters: sun, fish, cat, apple. The words are short, so every letter is big enough to trace, and they sit exactly on the lines the way children are taught to write them.
G1-430.p2: This page links a picture to its spoken word and then to its written word. First the child traces the picture. Then the child says its name aloud, which helps to hear the sounds in the word. Finally the child traces the word letter by letter, following the same lines used for handwriting. Because the four pictures are things every child names the same way, the word always matches what the child says. Point to each letter while saying the word slowly, and let the child try writing the word again beside the card.
G1-430.p3: This printable PDF suits first grade and the end of kindergarten, where tracing pictures meets early writing. It is the only page in the set with words, and the words are written for each language rather than translated. After this page, the trace-it-then-draw trailer page invites the child to add a drawing of their own. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

G1-431.h1: Trace the Picture, Then Draw: What Is in the Trailer?
G1-431.title: Trace the Picture, Then Draw: What Is in the Trailer? | PDF
G1-431.metaDescription: Trace a farm road with a tractor, an empty trailer, a goat, a goose and a cow, then draw what the tractor is carrying today. Trace and draw for 1st grade. PDF.
G1-431.p1: A tractor drives along a country road, pulling a trailer, and the trailer is empty. Behind the road gentle hills roll across the page under a sun and a cloud, and on the grass in front a goat, a goose and a cow look on. The whole farm scene is drawn in fine dashes: the tractor with its big wheels, the trailer, the road, the hills and the animals. Above the trailer there is a large open space, waiting for the child's own drawing.
G1-431.p2: This is the one page in the set with no single right answer. After tracing the farm, the child decides what the tractor is carrying today and draws it in the trailer: hay, pumpkins, a horse, a birthday cake or anything else. Tracing first warms up the hand; drawing afterwards lets the child use that control freely and makes the page their own. Ask the child to tell you about the drawing, because explaining a picture is good practice for speaking and, later, for writing a short story.
G1-431.p3: This printable PDF suits first grade and confident kindergarteners. Compare the finished pages of a whole class: every trailer carries something different. For a page that also ends in the child's own work, try the trace-and-color picnic. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

G1-432.h1: Symmetry Picture Tracing: Trace the Other Half
G1-432.title: Symmetry Picture Tracing: Trace the Other Half | PDF
G1-432.metaDescription: A butterfly in an open book and an owl, a bell and a koala in three mirrors: the left half is drawn, the right half is dashed. Trace the other half. 1st grade PDF.
G1-432.p1: At the top of the page a big butterfly spreads across an open book, its body lying along the book's spine. Below the book stand three arched mirrors, holding an owl, a bell and a koala's face. In every picture the left half is drawn in solid lines and the right half in dashes, and a thin line down the middle marks where the halves meet. Each picture is a drawing whose two halves really do match, measured line by line before it was chosen.
G1-432.p2: Finishing the other half asks the child to look at one side and make the other side the same, the first step towards understanding symmetry. The dashed half is the picture's own right side, so when the tracing is done both halves match exactly. Talk about it while tracing: does the butterfly's right wing look like its left wing? Has the owl got two eyes and two wings? Checking the finished picture against the solid half shows the child that a mirror line divides a picture into two parts that fit together.
G1-432.p3: This printable PDF suits first grade and children who enjoy a little challenge in their tracing. It works well before a lesson on mirror images or as a follow-up to folding paper butterflies. For a page where only small parts are missing, try the finish-the-picture shelf. Picture tracing follows the outline of whole pictures; abstract line practice, step-by-step drawing and numbered dot-to-dot have their own pages.

G1-433.h1: Animal Tracing Pictures: Find the 5 Hidden Animals
G1-433.title: Animal Tracing Pictures: Find the 5 Hidden Animals | PDF
G1-433.metaDescription: A busy autumn forest drawn in solid lines hides five dashed animals: an owl, a squirrel, a fox, a rabbit and a mouse. Find them and trace them. 1st grade PDF.
G1-433.p1: This page shows a busy forest in autumn. Big trees spread their crowns across the page, leaves are scattered over the branches and the ground, mushrooms and flowers grow along a winding path, and grass covers the forest floor. All of this is drawn in solid black lines. Hidden in the forest are five animals drawn in dashes: an owl in a tree, a squirrel in the leaves, a fox beside the path, a rabbit among the flowers and a mouse near the mushrooms.
G1-433.p2: First the child has to find the animals. That means looking carefully through a busy picture and telling the dashed lines apart from the solid ones, a skill called figure-ground perception that also helps children pick out letters on a crowded page. Each animal has a little clear space around it, so once it is found it can be traced without bumping into other lines. The instruction says there are five, and there are exactly five, so the child knows when the search is complete. Count them together at the end.
G1-433.p3: This printable PDF suits first grade and is a great autumn activity, though the forest works in any season. After tracing, the solid forest and the dashed animals make a detailed picture to color. For counting with tracing at kindergarten level, try the ducks on the pond.
